name: Glaucous
lede: Glaucous is an old botanical and literary word for a dull, grey-tinged blue-green, which the charts and the web later pinned to a clearer, bluer swatch.

sections.title: What the word meant
sections.body:
The word builds on the prefix *glauc-*, which Paterson marks as Latin and glosses as grey or silvery, bluish-grey, and in Roman times possibly even yellow [1]. His entry for the English word reads: a light greenish blue, a dull greenish blue used of the sea, or covered with a bloom like the dusting on a plum [1]. St Clair's glossary of color words says only: pale grey blue-green [2].

Paterson also links the word to the Indo-European root behind gold, glistening and yolk, which fits the Roman range from silvery to yellow [3]. The books agree on the family, a grey-leaning sea green, and disagree on how blue it should be.

In St Clair's account of green, a glaucous shade is called the darling of the Art Deco movement [4].

sections.title: The swatch is bluer than the word
sections.body:
The swatch here is a clear mid blue, which does not match the dictionary senses above [1][2]. It comes from Ridgway's 1912 plate XLI, and ISCC-NBS 1955 calls it a brilliant purplish blue, 8.3 units away; Maerz and Paul record the name from 1671 [5]. The nearest named color is [[steel-blue]], 5.5 units off [5].

If you want the grey-green of a cabbage leaf or a juniper berry, look toward [[sea-green]] and [[blue-green]] instead. The word has always been looser than its web swatch, and the gap is the main thing to remember about it.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Glaucous is a modest presence in paint: 122 of 23,781 paintings in our archive (0.51 per cent), 69 by the stricter within-painting lens, more common than 54 per cent of named colors [6]. Inside a painting it is usually an accent, in 59 per cent of those 69 [6].

It peaks in the 1900s, in 14 of 1,674 paintings, 1.9 times the museums' baseline [6]. The earliest match is a 1405 painting by Spinello Aretino, a look-alike hue 507 years before the name's first record in our sources, 1912 [6]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a color match is a look-alike hue and not a pigment test. [6]
